packet.description_seed: The latest update from the US Food and Drug Administration means the exact source of the parasite is still not known.

what: Test that found source of US explosive diarrhoea outbreak was false positive, health officials say

clean_source_blocks.text: Tests of an iceberg lettuce sample for the parasite that has caused an explosive diarrhoea outbreak affecting thousands of people in the US produced a false positive, officials have now said. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Saturday reported that the sample from food supplier Taylor Farms, which supplies the Taco Bell food chain, had tested positive for cyclospora. It said on Sunday that it had re-reviewed the sample and reported the false-positive to Taylor Farms, adding it "continues working with the firm to ensure product implicated in this outbreak has been removed from the market". The latest update means the exact source of the parasite is still not known. No deaths have been reported from cyclosporiasis infections, but at least 94 people have been hospitalised.
The latest update from the US Food and Drug Administration means the exact source of the parasite is still not known.

Cyclospora, a parasite that causes “explosive” diarrhea, has surged to unusually high levels this year, as dozens of states face outbreaks and authorities race to trace the source or sources. The intestinal infection typically peaks between May and August, but this year may be shaping up to be the worst outbreak some experts have seen. According to the latest numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been nearly 7,000 confirmed and probable cyclosporiasis cases in the U.S. this year, compared to about 3,000 in previous years. “It’s kind of surprising how big this is. ... I think this is going to be the largest ever in the U.S.,” Dr. Chuck Gerba, microbiologist and professor of virology in the department of environmental science at the University of Arizona, tells TODAY.com.

The broader rise in confirmed cases across 34 states points to more than one outbreak, said Donald Prater, DVM, the FDA's acting Deputy Commissioner for Food, during the briefing. "I think we're looking at multiple clusters and subclusters." The FDA is aware of a "signal" pointing to lettuce as a possible outbreak source in Michigan, said. "We're continuing to trace multiple items, including lettuce." State officials in Michigan reported on July 14 that the count in their state is 3,309 confirmed patients. Those state officials reported on July 13 that they believe lettuce and/or salad mixes are the source of the parasite, but they said there is no single grower, supplier or brand identified yet. New York and Ohio are each reporting several hundred confirmed patients.

Tests of an iceberg lettuce sample for the parasite that has caused an explosive diarrhoea outbreak affecting thousands of people in the US produced a false positive, officials have now said.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Saturday reported that the sample from food supplier Taylor Farms, which supplies the Taco Bell food chain, had tested positive for cyclospora.

It said on Sunday that it had re-reviewed the sample and reported the false-positive to Taylor Farms, adding it "continues working with the firm to ensure product implicated in this outbreak has been removed from the market".

The latest update means the exact source of the parasite is still not known.

No deaths have been reported from cyclosporiasis infections, but at least 94 people have been hospitalised.

Taylor Farms announced on Friday that it was voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce from the US market sourced from central Mexico, and issued a list of affected products.

The FDA reported the following day that the positive sample was taken from a product not part of Taylor Farms' current recall announced on Friday.

A recall differs from a voluntary product removal in that it requires a company to notify customers and recover affected products from commerce, making it a broader and more costly corrective action.

The FDA said it collected the sample during targeted surveillance of the import as part of its investigation into the outbreak.

It said on Sunday: "Due to the complexity in detection of Cyclospora, FDA laboratory experts re-reviewed the sample results and have concluded that the finding does not represent true amplification and should be considered a false positive," the FDA said in Sunday's statement.

The infections were first detected on 13 May, according to the FDA.

Symptoms of the foodborne illness can take up to two weeks to present. They include watery diarrhoea that lasts for days, sudden weight loss, and a loss of appetite.

Thousands of people have been infected with Cyclospora linked to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms and sold at Taco Bell locations in at least five states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The CDC advises not to eat shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia.

The fast food chain said it had completed its removal of affected Taylor Farms lettuce from its restaurants.

[Lähde: Food Safety News | URL: https://www.foodsafetynews.com/2026/07/cdc-says-thousands-are-likely-infected-with-cyclospora-parasite/]
The CDC is reporting that almost 7,000 people nationwide are part of several outbreaks of infections from the microscopic cyclospora parasite.

The foodborne parasite has infected people in 34 states according to a July 14 report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The agency had previously been reporting 843 confirmed patients. Now the CDC is reporting that there are 5,100 more suspected patients. By this time in 2025 the CDC had counted 249 confirmed patients.

This year's case count "is a much higher number than we typically see in a cyclosporiasis season," Gwen Biggerstaff,  deputy director of CDC's Division of Foodborne, Waterborne, and Environmental Diseases said during a media briefing Tuesday. "It's a very big shift from what we've seen in previous seasons."

The broader rise in confirmed cases across 34 states points to more than one outbreak, said Donald Prater, DVM, the FDA's acting Deputy Commissioner for Food, during the briefing. "I think we're looking at multiple clusters and subclusters."

The FDA is aware of a "signal" pointing to lettuce as a possible outbreak source in Michigan, said. "We're continuing to trace multiple items, including lettuce."

State officials in Michigan reported on July 14 that the count in their state is 3,309 confirmed patients. Those state officials reported on July 13 that they believe lettuce and/or salad mixes are the source of the parasite, but they said there is no single grower, supplier or brand identified yet.

New York and Ohio are each reporting several hundred confirmed patients.

The CDC’s counting has been hampered by the fact that the agency stopped tracking cyclospora infections beginning July 1 in 2025.

This year's count comes a year after program cuts led by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. prompted the CDC to remove the microscopic parasite Cyclospora from a list of eight pathogens that states were mandated to report to the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, or FoodNet. As of July 2025, reporting is optional for all pathogens except Salmonella and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.

“For weeks the distance between what the states were counting and what Atlanta was publishing was the whole story; this week the agency finally revised upward, pushed the alert to every clinician and lab in the country, and named the outbreak. That is what a functioning surveillance system is supposed to do,” said food safety expert and attorney Bill Marler.

payload.title: Yhdysvaltain syklosporaepidemian lähde yhä avoinna – salaattinäytteen tulos oli virheellinen
payload.summary: Jäävuorisalaatista saatu positiivinen syklosporatulos osoittautui virheelliseksi. Yhdysvalloissa on tänä vuonna kirjattu lähes 7 000 vahvistettua tai todennäköistä tapausta.
payload.content:
Yhdysvaltain elintarvike- ja lääkevirasto FDA on perunut tiedon, jonka mukaan tuhansien ihmisten syklosporatartuntoihin liittyvän epidemian mahdollinen lähde olisi löytynyt jäävuorisalaatista. Näytteen uudelleentarkastus osoitti positiivisen tuloksen virheelliseksi, joten voimakasta ripulia aiheuttavan loisen tarkka lähde tai mahdolliset useat lähteet ovat yhä selvittämättä.

## Salaattinäytteen tulos muuttui

FDA ilmoitti lauantaina, että elintarviketoimittaja Taylor Farmsilta peräisin olleesta jäävuorisalaattinäytteestä oli löytynyt Cyclospora-loista. Taylor Farms toimittaa tuotteita muun muassa Taco Bell -ravintolaketjulle. Virasto kertoi kuitenkin sunnuntaina tarkastaneensa näytteen uudelleen ja ilmoittaneensa yhtiölle, että alkuperäinen testitulos oli väärä positiivinen.

FDA:n mukaan se jatkaa yhteistyötä Taylor Farmsin kanssa varmistaakseen, että epidemiaan liitetty tuote on poistettu markkinoilta. Korjattu tulos ei siis päätä viranomaisten jäljitystyötä: yhtäkään kasvattajaa, toimittajaa tai tuotemerkkiä ei ole vahvistettu tartuntojen lähteeksi. FDA on saanut Michiganista viitteen, jonka perusteella salaatti voi liittyä ainakin osaan sairastumisista, mutta havainto ei vielä yksilöi tiettyä tuotetta. Virasto jäljittää edelleen useita elintarvikkeita, niiden joukossa salaattia.

## Tapauksia lähes 7 000

Yhdysvaltain tautikeskuksen CDC:n uusimpien lukujen mukaan maassa on tänä vuonna kirjattu lähes 7 000 vahvistettua tai todennäköistä syklosporatapausta. Vertailuksi aiempina vuosina tapauksia on ollut noin 3 000. Ainakin 94 sairastunutta on joutunut sairaalahoitoon, mutta syklosporatartuntoihin liittyviä kuolemia ei ole ilmoitettu.

Suolistoinfektion aiheuttava Cyclospora-loinen tunnetaan rajusta ripulista. Tartunnat ovat tavallisesti yleisimmillään toukokuun ja elokuun välillä, mutta tämän vuoden tapausmäärä on noussut poikkeuksellisen suureksi. Arizonan yliopiston ympäristötieteiden osaston mikrobiologi ja virologian professori Chuck Gerba kuvasi laajuutta yllättäväksi ja arvioi, että epidemiasta saattaa tulla Yhdysvaltain tähän asti suurin.

## Michiganissa tuhansia tapauksia

Tapauksia on todettu 34 osavaltiossa, mikä FDA:n elintarvikeasioista vastaavan virkaa tekevän apulaiskomissaarin Donald Praterin mukaan viittaa useisiin epidemioihin sekä tartuntaryppäisiin ja niiden alaryhmiin. Michiganissa oli 14. heinäkuuta mennessä vahvistettu 3 309 sairastunutta. Osavaltion viranomaiset ilmoittivat 13. heinäkuuta epäilevänsä lähteeksi salaattia tai salaattisekoituksia, mutta eivät ole tunnistaneet yhtä kasvattajaa, toimittajaa tai tuotemerkkiä. New York ja Ohio ovat kumpikin ilmoittaneet useista sadoista vahvistetuista tapauksista.
summary_bullets: Yhdysvalloissa on kirjattu tänä vuonna lähes 7 000 vahvistettua tai todennäköistä tapausta.
Viranomaiset tutkivat useita tartuntaryppäitä, eikä yhtä lähdettä, toimittajaa tai tuotemerkkiä ole vahvistettu.

Tapauksia on todettu 34 osavaltiossa, mikä FDA:n elintarvikeasioista vastaavan virkaa tekevän apulaiskomissaarin Donald Praterin mukaan viittaa useisiin epidemioihin sekä tartuntaryppäisiin ja niiden alaryhmiin. Michiganissa oli 14. heinäkuuta mennessä vahvistettu 3 309 sairastunutta. Osavaltion viranomaiset ilmoittivat 13. heinäkuuta epäilevänsä lähteeksi salaattia tai salaattisekoituksia, mutta eivät ole tunnistaneet yhtä kasvattajaa, toimittajaa tai tuotemerkkiä. New York ja Ohio ovat kumpikin ilmoittaneet useista sadoista vahvistetuista tapauksista.

article.source_text:
Tests of an iceberg lettuce sample for the parasite that has caused an explosive diarrhoea outbreak affecting thousands of people in the US produced a false positive, officials have now said. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Saturday reported that the sample from food supplier Taylor Farms, which supplies the Taco Bell food chain, had tested positive for cyclospora. It said on Sunday that it had re-reviewed the sample and reported the false-positive to Taylor Farms, adding it "continues working with the firm to ensure product implicated in this outbreak has been removed from the market". The latest update means the exact source of the parasite is still not known. No deaths have been reported from cyclosporiasis infections, but at least 94 people have been hospitalised.

The latest update from the US Food and Drug Administration means the exact source of the parasite is still not known.

Cyclospora, a parasite that causes “explosive” diarrhea, has surged to unusually high levels this year, as dozens of states face outbreaks and authorities race to trace the source or sources. The intestinal infection typically peaks between May and August, but this year may be shaping up to be the worst outbreak some experts have seen. According to the latest numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been nearly 7,000 confirmed and probable cyclosporiasis cases in the U.S. this year, compared to about 3,000 in previous years. “It’s kind of surprising how big this is. ... I think this is going to be the largest ever in the U.S.,” Dr. Chuck Gerba, microbiologist and professor of virology in the department of environmental science at the University of Arizona, tells TODAY.com.

The broader rise in confirmed cases across 34 states points to more than one outbreak, said Donald Prater, DVM, the FDA's acting Deputy Commissioner for Food, during the briefing. "I think we're looking at multiple clusters and subclusters." The FDA is aware of a "signal" pointing to lettuce as a possible outbreak source in Michigan, said. "We're continuing to trace multiple items, including lettuce." State officials in Michigan reported on July 14 that the count in their state is 3,309 confirmed patients. Those state officials reported on July 13 that they believe lettuce and/or salad mixes are the source of the parasite, but they said there is no single grower, supplier or brand identified yet. New York and Ohio are each reporting several hundred confirmed patients.
